John Bramhall
jon bram'hawl
n. (John Bramhall, 1594–1663, bishop of Derry and archbishop of Armagh)
Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious, through John; English Bramhall, from a Cheshire place-name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

John Bramhall was the ablest of the Laudian party in Ireland and the chief instrument of its policy. Brought over by Lord Deputy Wentworth in 1633, he recovered a great deal of alienated church property, which was a real reform, and used the same energy to impose the English Articles and canons on the Irish church in place of the Irish Articles of 1615, to enforce ceremonial conformity, and to drive the Scots Presbyterian ministers of Ulster out of their parishes. He also wrote a formidable defence of free will against Thomas Hobbes. He went into exile in the civil war and returned as archbishop of Armagh in 1661. The dictionary honours the writing against Hobbes and names the policy as what it was (Act 5:29).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines conformity as compliance with established usages, and canon as a law or rule of ecclesiastical discipline.

expand to see more

CONFORM'ITY, n. Correspondence with a model or pattern; compliance with established usages or customs.

CAN'ON, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, a law or rule of doctrine or discipline, enacted by a council.

CER'EMONIAL, a. Relating to ceremony or external rite; ritual; according to the forms of established rites.

DEPRIVE', v.t. To divest of an office or dignity; to depose; to take away from.

Key Scripture

Act 5:29 — "Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men."

Act 4:19 — "But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye."

Rom 13:1 — "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God."

Mat 22:21 — "They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's."

Modern Corruption

He recovered the church's lands and drove the Ulster Presbyterians out of their parishes.

expand to see more

The error is named precisely and it is not that Bramhall held episcopal government, which was the Church of Ireland's settled order and no scandal in itself. It is that he used the civil power to deprive faithful preaching ministers of their congregations over ceremonies that Scripture nowhere commands, in a country starved of preaching. The regulative principle of worship cuts exactly here: what God has not commanded in his worship may not be imposed, and least of all imposed by a magistrate's warrant on pain of a man's livelihood.

The principle to recover is that obedience to the magistrate is real and bounded by obedience to God. “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). The apostles put the question back to the council rather than answering for it: “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19). The power itself is ordained: “the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1). And the spheres are divided: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek peitharcheo (G3980), to obey one in authority; Greek exousia (G1849), authority, jurisdiction.

Greek peitharcheo (G3980) — to obey one in authority, to submit to rule; Acts 5:29.

Greek mallon (G3123) — rather, more, in preference to; Acts 5:29.

Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, delegated power, jurisdiction; Romans 13:1.

Greek hupotasso (G5293) — to subject, to place under; Romans 13:1.

Greek apodidomi (G591) — to render, to give back what is due; Matthew 22:21.

Usage

"“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — the Ulster ministers deprived."

"“Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's” (Mat 22:21) — and the spheres divided."

"“the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1) — ordained, and bounded."
